questions.q: State two key properties of the normal distribution curve.
questions.target: Properties of the normal distribution
questions.answer: The normal distribution curve is symmetric (bell-shaped) about its mean $\mu$, and the total area under the curve equals 1. (Other valid properties: mean = median = mode; the curve is asymptotic to the horizontal axis.)
questions.explanation: The normal distribution curve is symmetric (bell-shaped) about its mean $\mu$, and the total area under the curve equals 1. (Other valid properties: mean = median = mode; the curve is asymptotic to the horizontal axis.)

questions.q: Explain what it means for the normal distribution curve to be "asymptotic" to the horizontal axis.
questions.target: Properties of the normal distribution
questions.answer: It means the curve approaches the horizontal axis as $x\rightarrow\pm\infty$ but never actually touches or crosses it — the probability density gets arbitrarily close to zero but is never exactly zero for any finite $x$.
questions.explanation: It means the curve approaches the horizontal axis as $x\rightarrow\pm\infty$ but never actually touches or crosses it — the probability density gets arbitrarily close to zero but is never exactly zero for any finite $x$.

questions.q: State one similarity and one difference between the normal distribution and the discrete uniform distribution.
questions.target: Properties of the normal distribution
questions.answer: Similarity: both are probability distributions in which the total probability sums (or integrates) to 1. Difference: the normal distribution is continuous and bell-shaped, with values clustering near the mean, while the discrete uniform distribution is discrete and every outcome has equal probability.
questions.explanation: Similarity: both are probability distributions in which the total probability sums (or integrates) to 1. questions.q: A random variable $X\sim B(200,0.4)$ is to be approximated by a normal distribution. State the mean and variance to use, and check the approximation is valid (both $np$ and $n(1-p)$ should exceed 5).
questions.target: The normal approximation to the binomial distribution
questions.answer: $np=200(0.4)=80$ and $n(1-p)=200(0.6)=120$, both exceed 5, so the approximation is valid. Use $X\approx N(80,48)$, since $\mathrm{Var}(X)=np(1-p)=200(0.4)(0.6)=48$.
questions.explanation: $np=200(0.4)=80$ and $n(1-p)=200(0.6)=120$, both exceed 5, so the approximation is valid. Use $X\approx N(80,48)$, since $\mathrm{Var}(X)=np(1-p)=200(0.4)(0.6)=48$.

questions.q: State the two conditions required to approximate a binomial distribution $X \sim B(n, p)$ by a normal distribution.
questions.target: Normal Approximation to the Binomial Distribution
questions.answer: The standard Cambridge AS Level guideline requires both $np > 5$ and $n(1 - p) > 5$ for an adequate normal approximation.
questions.explanation: The standard Cambridge AS Level guideline requires both $np > 5$ and $n(1 - p) > 5$ for an adequate normal approximation.

questions.q: A fair coin is tossed 100 times. Using the normal approximation with continuity correction, what is the expression for $P(X \geq 55)$?
questions.target: Normal Approximation to the Binomial Distribution
questions.answer: $\mu = 100(0.5) = 50$, $\sigma^2 = 100(0.5)(0.5) = 25$. For $X \geq 55$, the continuity correction shifts to the left boundary: $P(Y > 54.5)$.
questions.explanation: $\mu = 100(0.5) = 50$, $\sigma^2 = 100(0.5)(0.5) = 25$. For $X \geq 55$, the continuity correction shifts to the left boundary: $P(Y > 54.5)$.
